prompt:
The GAL-TAN framework identifies political orientation on a single axis. Individuals and texts are placed according to the degree to which their views align with either pole, as follows:

  - Individuals at the GAL (Green/Alternative/Libertarian) pole support expanded
    personal freedoms and social liberalisation, for example: access to abortion,
    same-sex marriage, environmental protection, and multiculturalism.

  - Individuals at the TAN (Traditional/Authoritarian/Nationalist) pole prioritise
    order, tradition, and stability, and believe that the state should treat the
    maintenance of national identity as a priority, for example: restrictive
    immigration policy, emphasis on law and order, defence of traditional social
    institutions, and national sovereignty over supranational authority.

A text occupies a position on this axis to the extent that it argues FROM these commitments, not to the extent that it mentions the associated topics:

  - Environmental or immigration policy discussed in administrative or fiscal
    terms does not by itself indicate a position.
  - Nuclear expansion argued for energy security is not GAL.
  - Faster asylum processing argued on humanitarian grounds is not TAN.

The profile below describes the positional priorities of the British electorate.

<profile>
  gal: 0.45
  tan: 0.55
</profile>

Below are two texts.

TEXT_D:
Summary of proposals (2001)

Health
- Cut waiting times by recruiting 27,500 nurses, 4,600 doctors, 10,250 allied health professionals; add 10,000 hospital beds.
- Improve retention with average £1,000 pay rises for lowest-paid NHS staff; commission on NHS pay and conditions.
- Free personal care for elderly/long-term patients; restore free dental and eye checks; double investment in scanners; £500m to guarantee NHS dentistry access.
- Create a Pharmaceutical Agency to end “postcode lottery,” use NHS purchasing power, and move toward scrapping prescription charges.
- Patient Care Guarantees; stronger local accountability; independent advocacy (incl. Children’s Rights Commissioner); no-fault compensation; end mixed wards; ban age discrimination in care.

Education, skills and work
- Primary classes averaged at 25; recruit 5,000 extra secondary teachers; 40,000 classroom assistants (25,000 in Key Stage 1); two paid prep hours weekly for primary teachers; paid training salary for trainees; reduce bureaucracy and testing at age 7.
- Abolish university tuition fees; restore grants for poorer students; raise loan repayment threshold; oppose top-up fees; improve HE staff pay.
- Adult entitlement to funded tuition (to Level 2; to Level 3 for 16–24s); merge skills funders into a Learning Council; SME training incentives; paid study leave for 16–24s; replace New Deal with a Flexible Guarantee via a combined Benefits and Jobs Agency.

Law, order and justice
- 6,000 additional police officers; 2,000 part-time retained community officers; Community Safety Force for low-level disorder.
- Independent police complaints system; community-focused partnerships; cooperation with Europol.
- Shift from costly prison expansion to effective alternatives; full working day, skills and rehabilitation in prisons; reduce reoffending.
- Stronger victims’ rights (impact statements, information); tackle hate crimes; retain jury trial; end most mandatory sentencing; expand restorative and youth justice reforms.

Transport
- Free off-peak local bus travel for pensioners and disabled people; aim half-price fares for under-19s in education.
- Abolish Vehicle Excise Duty for the cleanest vehicles; higher VED for most polluting; no real-terms rise in fuel duty next Parliament.
- Enable local funding tools (bonds, congestion charging, parking levies); create a Sustainable Transport Authority; stronger public control of rail investment and safety; restructure rail infrastructure into a not-for-profit public-interest model; rural transport fund; priority to road maintenance and safety; not-for-profit air traffic control; tighter night flight limits.

Pensions, wages and benefits
- Increase basic state pension (£5/week single; more for over-75s/80s; proportional rises for couples); scrap savings penalty; establish an Independent Pensions Authority; relax annuity rules; develop personal second pensions and extend basic entitlement over time.
- Annual review of the minimum wage; single full rate from age 16.
- Extra £200 for children in families on long-term income support; replace the Child Support Agency with family courts.
- Improve support for disabled people (incl. winter fuel payments for the severely disabled); simplify housing benefit; fairer utility tariffs; better cold weather payments; reduce tax on the lowest paid over time.

Culture, media and sport
- Embed arts in schools; restore free instrumental tuition funding; lower VAT on renovation (and apply low rate to new build); universal free internet access in libraries.
- Create OFCOM; redefine public service broadcasting; reform BBC governance; tighter cross-media ownership; community sports plans.

Business, consumers and environment
- Scrap unnecessary regulations; small business rates allowance; stronger competition law; improved consumer and bank protections; Post Office universal service.
- Replace the Climate Change Levy with a carbon tax; emissions trading; at least 10% renewable energy by 2010 rising annually; phase out nuclear as stations retire; expand research funding; ethical corporate reporting.

Political and civil rights
- Referendum on AV+ for Westminster; STV for local/European elections; voting and candidacy from 16; elected Senate to replace the Lords; stronger parliamentary scrutiny; local income tax.
- Stronger Freedom of Information; Equality Act and Equality Commission; civil partnership registration; judicial oversight of surveillance; no ID cards.
- Fairer, faster asylum system; end vouchers; improve support and local compensation.

Communities, rural and housing
- National doorstep recycling (60% in 10 years); flood defence task force; GM crop moratorium until 2004; marine protected areas.
- One-stop regeneration grants; brownfield-first with planning and VAT reform; protect green spaces; require planning for mobile masts.
- Reform CAP/CFP toward sustainability and local co-management; support tenant and organic farming; create a Ministry for Rural Affairs; protect village services; measures on affordability, empty homes, and leasehold rights; option for site value rating.

Europe, defence and international
- EU constitutional settlement clarifying powers; subsidiarity and transparency; accountable Commission/Council; enlargement; single Parliament seat in Brussels.
- Maintain defence spending; flexible, deployable forces; retain minimum nuclear deterrent while pursuing disarmament; oppose national missile defence; moratorium on depleted uranium.
- End subsidies for arms exports; strengthen UN (incl. rapid reaction/disaster capacity, ICC); fairer WTO rules with environmental integration; aid to 0.7% GNI, untied and focused on gender, health (HIV/AIDS), and education; stronger climate commitments (e.g., CO2 −20% by 2010).

Economy and tax
- Enhance Bank of England independence (non-renewable MPC terms, transparent appointments).
- Enable euro entry via referendum at a competitive rate.
- Allow devolved/regional/local borrowing for investment.
- Fund priorities through 1p on income tax for education; 50% top rate above £100k for pensions and NHS; CGT simplification; Citizen’s Tax Contract; annual independent fiscal assessment; green tax reform matched by cuts elsewhere; reduce tax burden on lowest incomes over time.

TEXT_F:
Summary of 2001 manifesto proposals (ideological framing and names omitted)

- Family and education
  - Targeted tax cuts: higher Children’s Tax Credit for under‑5s; transferable allowance for couples with young children or caring responsibilities; remove tax on Widowed Parent benefits; reform in‑work credit to be paid to the caring parent.
  - School autonomy (“Free Schools”): heads/governors control staffing, pay, admissions via home–school agreements; easier exclusion for disruptive pupils with off-site Progress Centres; successful schools free to expand; new schools allowed from faith, parent, charitable and company providers; parents can trigger special inspections and management change; redirect bureaucracy savings directly to schools.
  - Students and universities: raise loan repayment threshold to £20,000; no top‑up fees; create university endowments.

- Crime and justice
  - Increase police numbers; cut bureaucracy; visible policing (e.g., paperwork done on the beat); parish constables; focus on antisocial behaviour.
  - Expand secure training places for persistent young offenders; link release to behaviour/qualifications.
  - Mandatory prison for selling drugs to under‑16s; tougher sentences near schools.
  - End automatic early release; require prison work with proceeds to victims/families.
  - Lifetime supervision available for sex offenders; protect children online.
  - Stronger victim rights: named contacts in police/CPS; written reasons if charges dropped; update self‑defence and double jeopardy rules.

- Economy and regulation
  - Tax reductions funded by £8bn in savings (excluding schools/NHS/police/defence): abolish taxes on most savings/dividends; raise pensioner personal allowance by £2,000; married couple’s allowance; higher Children’s Tax Credit for under‑5s; cut fuel duty by at least 6p/litre; business rates cuts; abolish IR35; targeted regeneration breaks; relief for approved share options.
  - Simpler, more transparent tax/accounts; Capital Gains Tax simplification with lower rates.
  - Deregulation Commission with departmental regulatory budgets; small-firm exemptions; focus utility regulators on competition.
  - Replace Climate Change Levy package; review nuclear’s role.
  - Keep the pound; bolster monetary policy independence; external fiscal scrutiny.

- Health
  - Match planned NHS funding but shift control to clinicians; Patient’s Guarantee of maximum waits based on clinical need with right to alternative NHS/private provision; more choice for patients/GPs; empower ward sisters/matrons; expand practice nurse roles; specialist surgical units; Exceptional Medicines Fund; increase hospice funding; remove tax penalties on private medical insurance when affordable.

- Older people and care
  - Raise basic state pension (larger uplift for over‑75s); option to consolidate certain payments into a higher tax‑free pension; increase age allowance by £2,000 to remove ~1m from income tax; abolish compulsory annuitisation at 75; explore funded pension option for younger workers; protect assets for those who pre‑fund long‑term care.

- International and defence
  - In the EU but retain veto; keep the pound; seek treaty flexibility/reserved powers; strengthen the single market and anti‑fraud measures.
  - Prioritise NATO; oppose separate EU military structures; maintain independent deterrent; support missile defence; reach full manning; reserves reform; exempt armed forces from certain human rights constraints as other states do.
  - Aid: work toward 0.7% GNP; double share via charities; improve EU aid or permit bilateral alternatives; push debt relief, HIV/AIDS, conflict resolution; envoy for religious freedom.
  - Trade: pursue EU‑NAFTA free trade area toward global free trade by 2020; align diplomacy and trade promotion.

- Asylum
  - House new applicants in secure reception centres pending decisions; presume refusal for safe‑country claims; create a removals agency for rejected cases.

- Welfare and civil society
  - Office of Civil Society; eliminate irrecoverable VAT for charities.
  - Replace existing job schemes with outcome‑based contracts paying for sustained employment; “can work, must work” principle; lone parents with children over 11 to seek suitable work.
  - Improve disabled savings rules; new Incapacity Benefit agency funding rehabilitation; national anti‑fraud squad; clean up National Insurance numbers.

- Town, country, transport, environment
  - Foot‑and‑mouth recovery plan; reform CAP/CFP with more national/local control; honest food labelling; reduce rural red tape; cut business rates for key rural services; benefit card to sustain post offices; support rural transport.
  - Abolish top‑down housebuilding targets; more local control; protect green/“blue belt” areas; rural affairs select committee.
  - Urban regeneration companies with powers over policing, schools, planning, and housing renewal; promote brownfield building; expand homeownership (right‑to‑buy, rent‑to‑mortgage, homesteading).
  - Transport: long‑term plans; Roads Standards Unit; consider 80mph where safe with strict enforcement; charge foreign lorries; revive rail; cut fuel duty; promote cleaner fuels/vehicles.
  - Environment: emissions trading, conservation, renewables, cleaner generation.

- Culture, media, sport
  - Privatise Channel 4; £3bn endowment for cultural bodies; simplify lottery rules; strengthen tourism promotion.
  - Protect school sport time/playing fields; charitable status for local sports clubs; streamline funding.
  - Single media/communications regulator; modernise ownership rules; independent BBC regulation; fair access for religious broadcasters.

- Democracy and governance
  - Devolve powers to high‑performing “free councils”; fewer central targets; local referendums on large council tax rises.
  - Abolish regional agencies/assemblies; return development powers locally.
  - English votes for English laws; strengthen Lords with independent appointments and elected element; enhance Commons scrutiny (more frequent PM accountability, stronger select committees); retain current general election voting system.
  - Reduce numbers of ministers, MPs (after scrutiny reforms), and political advisers.
